JPMorgan Chase (JPM), Visa (V), and Mastercard (MA) said on Thursday that some select customer data, including names and emails, was accessed by attackers after a cyberattack on a vendor. Spokespeople for the companies said no payments or card data was leaked and that their own systems were not affected by the incident. JPMorgan said it believes hackers who attacked a third-party vendor accessed marketing data, including customer names and email addresses. The bank also said the incident isn't related to outages many of its customers reported earlier this week, which it blamed on a software bug. "Based on our investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses," a JPMorgan spokesperson said. This price reflects trading activity during the overnight session on the Blue Ocean ATS, available 8 PM to 4 AM ET, Sunday through Thursday, when regular markets are closed. "We were recently informed of an incident at a third-party provider that resulted in the exposure of limited amount of email addresses – non-payments information – from a small subset of cardholders enrolled in a specific benefit program," a Mastercard spokesperson said. "There is no impact to the Mastercard payment network or the ability for people to use their cards," the person added. A Visa spokesperson added claims of the incident are associated to a third-party service provider in the Asia Pacific region. "This is unrelated to any of the system disruptions across different industries this past week," the Visa spokesperson added. A ransomware group known as n0n has claimed responsibility for the attacks on the dark web and shared sample data as proof, according to cybersecurity firm SOCRadar. The cybersecurity firm told Yahoo Finance that it hasn't independently verified whether the ransomware group carried out the intrusion. It also supported JPMorgan, Visa and Mastercard's statements that the breaches most likely originated at a third-party vendor and involved marketing and benefit-program data such as names and email addresses. "The most immediate risk for consumers is targeted phishing that impersonates their bank or card provider," SOCRadar chief information security officer Ensar Seker said in an emailed statement. The latest incident comes as consumers are on high alert after a string of major technology outages this November. title: J.P. Morgan sees Fed rate hikes at next three meetings as inflation persists - The Lufkin Daily News

FILE PHOTO: View of the facade as construction continues on the Federal Reserve Board building, in Washington, D.C., U.S., September 17, 2025. REUTERS/Ken Cedeno/File Photo Nov 19 (Reuters) - J.P. Morgan on Thursday said it expects the US Federal Reserve to deliver quarter-point rate hikes in January and March next year, on top of a previously forecast December increase, as sticky inflation keeps the need for further tightening in play. "These hikes aren't to deliver a bad labor market, but to preserve credibility when they have no compelling narrative for a pause," said J.P. Morgan strategists led by Michael Feroli. • Fed Chair Kevin Warsh has left the monetary policy path without an "overarching narrative," the brokerage said • "Without a narrative as a pole star, policy is more likely to be reactive to incoming data," it said • In a bid to control inflation, "almost all" policymakers agreed further rate hikes would be needed if the economy evolved as they expected, Fed meeting minutes showed on Wednesday • "The labor market has not been a source of inflationary pressure, and yet inflation remains elevated," J.P. Morgan said, adding it expects modest, positive job growth next year • Markets see a near-certain 25-basis-point increase in December and an 8% chance of a half-percentage-point move, according to the CME FedWatch tool • Brokerages BofA Global Research and Deutsche Bank also expect the central bank to hike rates at each of its next three meetings (Reporting by Joel Jose in Bengaluru; Editing by Shreya Biswas) Sorry, there are no recent results for popular images. title: JP Morgan Sends Apple Update Ahead of iPhone Upgrade Cycle - RealMoney Pro
content: It shows strong support for Apple’s premium iPhone models. While there is much attention on Anthropic’s (ANT) IPO and where its shares will open for trading on Thursday, a new global survey from JPMorgan Chase (JPM) finds consumer interest in Apple’s (AAPL) new iPhones are running at a multi-year high following the launch for the 18 Pro and Pro Max models. The “intent to buy” a new iPhone found 73% of those surveyed intend to so this year and that figure compares to 71% in 2025 and 68% in 2024. Breaking that down a bit, the “intent to buy” in 2026 figure for this year is 97%, up from 90%. While the figure is for U.S. compared to 63% last year, at 68% it’s well below the intent score for China. What factors are driving this reported intent? Better performance, camera upgrades and with a modest showing, AI features. We do need to point out that Apple began testing initial Apple Intelligence features in China earlier this month and those features are expected to be officially launched in China “during December.” 33% surveyed said they intended to buy an iPhone 18 Pro Max, with 20% leaning towards the iPhone 18 Pro and 14% citing the iPhone Duo was for them. While the iPhone 18 Pro Max was the most popular among global switchers from Android, 23% of switchers in the U.S. said they were doing so for the iPhone Duo. Part of what could be impacting the 2026 scores is that, so far, Apple has only brought the 18 Pro and Pro Max models to market. The iPhone 18 and the 18e models aren’t expected until early 2027 with the iPhone Air 2 to follow later in the year. We’ll begin our comments by saying that we want to be careful when assessing survey data as it hinges on the sample size and how the questions were being asked. As such, we view JPMorgan’s as helping support, at least so far, the iPhone upgrade cycle more because of the age of iPhone models in consumers hands than the allure of Siri AI and Apple Intelligence. Global smartphone replacement averages roughly 3.5 years, with shorter cycles in markets like China and Western Europe (around 33 months), and various estimate put the average age of an iPhone across geographic regions between 2.9 to 3.8 years, which suggest replacement demand will be a likely tailwind for Apple in 2027. Higher ASPs compared to prior models should also be a positive, but as we’ve discussed before, higher memory costs and Apple’s ability to mitigate them will dictate margin expectations and the degree of EPS growth in the coming quarters. We’re also interested to see what new CEO John Ternus has up his sleeve as the company comes off a large wave of product introductions over the last several weeks. At the time of publication, TheStreet Pro Portfolio was long AAPL shares. BY James "Rev Shark" DePorre · Nov 19, 2026, 4:28 PM EST

title: Visa, Mastercard, and JP Morgan Chase customer data reportedly compromised - WBAL News Radio
content: Data from thousands of Visa, Mastercard and JP Morgan Chase customers was leaked Thursday by a ransomware group, according to several reports. It’s the latest in a string of tech incidents that have unnerved customers across the U.S. over the past two weeks. Though the scope and source of the information remain unclear, The Wall Street Journal reports that thousands of customers’ data was involved. The incident has not disrupted payment services and is not linked to banking problems from earlier this week. JPMorgan Chase said Thursday that attackers targeted third-party service providers and may have accessed marketing data, including some customer names and email addresses. The bank said the incident was not connected to service disruptions customers experienced earlier in the week. title: Bank Customers Don't Trust AI With Their Money, And Citigroup (NYSE: C), JPMorgan (NYSE: JPM), And Schwab (NYSE: SCHW) Are Counting On It - Foreign Policy Journal
content: By David Prior | Nov 19, 2026 | Economy & Business, Featured, News & Analysis Only 49% of bank customers trust the accuracy of AI-generated financial information, compared with 79% who trust information sourced directly from bank websites, according to recent survey data. That credibility gap is proving to be a significant asset for major financial institutions as they push back against the growing ambitions of third-party AI agents seeking access to customer accounts. The conversation intensified following Meta Platforms’ (NASDAQ: META) September launch of Muse, a personal AI agent that drew widespread media attention and renewed speculation about artificial intelligence upending traditional banking. Concerns about Muse and similar tools center on scenarios where agents autonomously move money across accounts or exploit credit card reward systems at scale, potentially eroding core banking revenue streams. Yet the industry’s response has been less panic and more coordinated resistance, with several of the country’s largest financial institutions drawing clear boundaries around customer account access. Citigroup (NYSE: C), Bank of America (NYSE: BAC), and JPMorgan Chase (NYSE: JPM) have each announced they will refuse third-party AI agents or assistants permission to interact with customer accounts. Charles Schwab (NYSE: SCHW) CEO Rick Wurster struck a measured tone on the issue, telling Bloomberg last month that relatively few of the firm’s clients are even attempting to reach their accounts through unauthorized AI agents. A separate survey finding reinforces the banks’ position further, with 72% of customers expressing hesitation about sharing their financial data with generative AI tools at all. Without regulatory clarity defining the rules, liability frameworks, and permissible limits for agentic AI in financial services, banks are expected to maintain and potentially tighten those restrictions. The more telling strategic move, however, is what banks are building behind those walls, with institutions racing to develop proprietary AI products that keep customers engaged within their own ecosystems. Schwab has already unveiled an AI assistant called Charley, while JPMorgan has begun a targeted pilot of a tool named Smart Cash, designed to forecast users’ cash flow and automatically shift funds to maximize yield. By building in-house alternatives, banks are effectively using the competitive pressure from companies like Meta as a catalyst rather than a threat, channeling it into product development that strengthens customer retention. As one analyst put it plainly, “Banks are AI beneficiaries, not AI roadkill,” a framing that captures the industry’s current posture with notable precision. The emerging picture is one of an industry that has chosen to absorb and redirect technological disruption rather than cede ground to outside platforms competing for control of customer financial relationships. David Prior is a senior reporter at the Foreign Policy Journal, covering everything from current affairs and global politics to stock market news and analysis.

title: Hyundai Card, JP Morgan test AI agent treasury payments on DLT. Standards are the gap - Ledger Insights
content: Kinexys by JP Morgan has conducted a proof of concept in which an AI agent manages treasury liquidity in Hyundai Card’s blockchain deposit account. The agent was responsible for ensuring that a sufficient balance was maintained in Hyundai Card’s euro account. When the account needed topping up, the agent collected FX quotes and initiated a conversion from GBP to EUR. A Kinexys agent then checked the Hyundai Card agent’s identity and mandate before executing the trade. As a proof of concept the transactions were simulated, but the exercise was as much about governance as payments. The trial highlights three requirements. The Hyundai Card agent had to prove it was acting for Hyundai Card, which is a digital identity question. It also needed a mandate setting out which transactions it could execute. In the Kinexys design the agent drafts its own mandate, but only the company can approve it. After that, most transactions run automatically and only exceptions go to a human, which matters given the speed at which agents work. Finally, every transaction has to be auditable after the fact. Notably, a paper published by JP Morgan identifies the need for a common trust framework across the industry for working with agents. That’s essential for multibank payments. It calls for collaboration between clients, regulators and ecosystem partners. However, it does not refer to the standards bodies already working on the problem. Want the full story? title: JP Morgan and Hyundai Card Tests AI-Powered Payments Without Humans - CryptoPotato
content: JP Morgan Chase and South Korea’s Hyundai Card are testing AI agents that can negotiate financial transactions and make payments without direct human involvement. While the project could change how corporate payments work, JP Morgan’s early findings suggest that controlling autonomous systems may be harder than building them. According to a CNBC report, the two companies completed an initial proof of concept involving a simulated foreign exchange transaction in which a Hyundai Card AI agent requested a currency exchange to maintain euro liquidity in its deposit account on JP Morgan’s blockchain-based banking platform, Kinexys. The collaboration targets machine-to-machine payments, where AI systems, without a person in the loop, recommend actions, initiate and approve transfers, and verify their authenticity. A second phase, planned for the first half of 2027, will look at how multiple AI agents can interact, negotiate agreements, and settle payments with one another. Wee Kee Toh, global head of Kinexys Insights, told CNBC that the goal is to see what happens when agents move beyond just carrying out tasks and start dealing with each other. The technical challenge includes ensuring that these payment agents can sift through complex regulatory frameworks to stay within the laws of different jurisdictions, as well as detect fraud in real time. They must also handle edge cases that could confuse algorithms while maintaining clear audit trails to meet compliance requirements. However, the executive pointed out that developing the technology was the easy part, while establishing governance and internal controls could prove more difficult. According to a recent report by AvePoint, at least 34% of security breaches linked to AI agents were due to unauthorized autonomous actions, including them making transactions and data changes without human approval. Furthermore, AvePoint CEO Tianyi Jiang warned that interactions between AI agents could allow a compromised or malfunctioning agent to pass incorrect information to others and possibly trigger a chain of unauthorized actions. Recall that in October, OpenAI revealed that a research model took funds without permission from a developer’s wallet on the Ethereum testnet to pay for deployment fees. Regarding the concerns mentioned above, Toh pointed out that companies using the system can put guardrails around agents so that, for example, if an agent is authorized to transact up to $5 million, any requests above that amount will be rejected automatically. “You are going to draw a box around the agent. The agent will never be able to do anything out of the box,” he said. Alongside spending limits, Hassan Ahmed, Coinbase’s Singapore country director, added that safe agent payment should also have restricted account permissions and clear authorization requirements, and give users the ability to monitor activity and revoke access at any time. title: “Capital Has a Price Again,” Key Message from J.P. Morgan Private Bank for 2027 - Funds Society
content: Artificial intelligence, global fragmentation, and inflation are driving a historic repricing of capital, giving investors greater pricing power. This is the main conclusion of J.P. Morgan Private Bank’s 2027 global investment outlook report, “The Price of Progress.” “For much of the last cycle, investors could overlook the cost of capital. The next major phase of development demands paying closer attention to it. Today, technology companies, governments, and consumers compete for the same limited pool of capital, and it is investors who set its price. Every financing transaction must now clear a higher hurdle rate,” stated Grace Peters, Co-Head of Global Investment Strategy at J.P. Morgan Private Bank. For his part, Stephen Parker, Co-Head of Global Investment Strategy at J.P. Morgan Private Bank, added: “This pricing power puts investors in a position of strength, but it also makes capital allocation decisions carry greater consequences. Now that cash offers a real return, every investment must justify the capital allocated to it. The question is not simply where the opportunity lies, but where investors receive sufficient compensation for taking it on.” Regarding Europe, Oscar Carmona, Head of Investments at J.P. Morgan Private Bank in Spain, noted: “Europe has weathered rising energy costs and interest rates better than expected. We expect that resilience to hold in 2027. Inflation should moderate over time, but energy remains the decisive factor. If rising costs pass through to wages, food, and services, the downward path could be bumpy. We expect 2 additional rate hikes from the ECB, bringing the deposit facility rate (DFR) to 3% in early 2027, with limited room for much further tightening.” According to the firm, the “2027 Global Investment Outlook” report examines how investors must decide whom to lend to, which assets to invest in, and at what price, in an environment shaped by artificial intelligence, global fragmentation, and inflation. Throughout much of the post-financial crisis cycle, near-zero interest rates and quantitative easing policies kept financing costs low. However, this backdrop has changed. Inflation has remained above central bank targets throughout 2026, bond yields have reached multi-decade highs, and a global rate-hiking cycle has begun, with 17 of the 37 central banks we track currently oriented toward tightening monetary policy. Nevertheless, bond yields were already rising prior to monetary policy moves, underscoring the role investors now play in setting the price of capital. “Central banks will continue to play a pivotal role in 2027. How high rates go will matter, but policy rates do not tell the whole story. With investment-grade debt yields above 6% for the 1st time since the financial crisis, today’s starting point for high-credit-quality debt is more attractive than it has been in years, even if rates continue to rise,” Parker explained. He adds: “Higher yields reinforce the appeal of a traditional stock-and-bond portfolio, yet a balanced portfolio is only the starting point. Forward return outlooks for equities and fixed income are the most attractive in years, but uncertainty surrounding artificial intelligence, inflation risk, and historically high equity market concentration justify going further. Real assets, hedge funds, and private markets have shifted from a complement to a necessity.” Security, resilience, and regional alignment are increasingly taking precedence over efficiency. Governments—many already carrying elevated debt levels and fiscal deficits—need capital to bolster security, build out artificial intelligence ecosystems, and secure energy supply. As these demands grow, investors must make increasingly consequential choices about where to provide capital and on what terms. In this context, Peters stated: “Resilience is an enduring investment theme, but it will not deliver uniform returns across all markets. Assessing countries’ defense and artificial intelligence capabilities, their exposure to supply chain bottlenecks, and their vulnerability to climate change can help identify where capital may be best positioned in this era of global fragmentation. Given that every bloc faces vulnerabilities, concentrating investments in just 1 is likely unwise.” She continues: “In the United States, fiscal capacity and natural resources continue to underpin confidence in U.S. Treasuries and the dollar, whereas stronger corporate earnings in Europe make equities more attractive than sovereign debt. In Asia, South Korea and Taiwan play an essential role in semiconductor manufacturing, while Latin America offers opportunities ranging from nearshoring in Mexico to commodity exposure in other countries across the region.” Artificial intelligence infrastructure expansion remains constrained by resource scarcity rather than excess capacity, yet the debate is shifting from infrastructure capacity toward monetization and political risks. By the early 2030s, the global fleet of data centers will need to generate approximately $3T annually in end-customer revenue to reach breakeven. That is an ambitious target, though we believe the AI ecosystem can achieve it. Meanwhile, AI-related debt issuance is expected to exceed $300B this year. While it remains predominantly investment-grade debt, the emergence of newer, less transparent structures is driving up the cost of AI financing. “The boom can only continue if investors bridge the gap between infrastructure spending and sustainable revenue generation. Not every segment of the AI technology stack carries the same level of risk or warrants the same capital allocation. This requires making deliberate choices about where to invest within the AI ecosystem, rather than simply whether to participate in it,” Parker clarified. We believe hyperscalers offer the best exposure within public equities due to their ability to benefit from both compute scarcity and abundance scenarios. Conversely, the infrastructure and semiconductor segments warrant greater caution, particularly given growing political hurdles to data center construction. Regarding investment-grade AI-related debt, it provides the best risk-managed entry point, while the application layer, frontier AI labs, and AI-native software offer the most compelling long-term growth potential, best accessed selectively through private markets. title: JPMorgan is working on AI agent transactions that don’t involve humans - CNBC
content:
Artificial intelligence agents have already proven to be helpful, or cause a lot of trouble, or both. One area seen as high-potential is in payments, where — if they’re able to be trusted — the agents could deal with all sorts of money matters on behalf of people. That’s why JPMorgan Chase and South Korea’s Hyundai Card are testing how AI agents can handle financial transactions without direct human intervention, including whether they can eventually negotiate and make payments with one another. The companies have completed an initial proof-of-concept involving a simulated foreign exchange transaction and are targeting the first half of 2027 for a more complex phase involving multiple AI agents. Wee Kee Toh, global head of Kinexys Insights at Kinexys by JP Morgan, told CNBC that the next step is to test what happens when autonomous agents move beyond execution and begin interacting with each other in an ecosystem. “That, I would say, is really the biggest part of what we want to get as an expansion of the phase one scope,” he added. The initial trial involved a Hyundai Card AI agent requesting a foreign exchange transaction to maintain euro liquidity in its Kinexys blockchain deposit account. JPMorgan said it was the first private blockchain-based autonomous bank-agent-to-client-agent test for corporate treasury management. While the initial trial has been completed, JPMorgan has yet to set a timeline for commercializing the technology. Toh said building the technology itself was relatively straightforward, but establishing appropriate governance and internal controls proved more difficult. “Technology-wise, it’s really not the biggest hurdle,” he said, pointing instead to questions around accountability and the risks of allowing AI agents to execute financial transactions without direct human oversight. However, the potential of such agents to change interactions with financial services has to come with equivalent accountability, according to experts. Data management and protection software company AvePoint found in its State of AI 2026 report that unauthorized autonomous agent actions were the third most common AI agent-related security breach, affecting 34.1% of companies that reported such incidents. Those actions included executing transaction and modifying data without approval, though the findings were not isolated to corporate treasury payments. “When agents negotiate and execute autonomously … governance shifts from monitoring human behavior to monitoring machine-to-machine dependencies,” said AvePoint CEO Tianyi Jiang. Jiang explained that interacting AI agents could amplify errors and trigger transactions before humans can intervene. “The worst-case scenario is a cascading failure where one compromised or hallucinating agent feeds bad data to another,” he said, potentially “triggering a high-speed chain reaction of flawed financial transfers before a human even realizes it is happening.” To address such concerns, Kinexys developed a framework that restricts AI agents to predefined transaction parameters, automatically rejecting requests that fall outside authorized limits. “You are going to draw a box around the agent. The agent will never be able to do anything out of the box,” Toh said. For example, an AI agent authorized to transact up to $5 million would be blocked from executing transactions above that threshold, he said. Hassan Ahmed, Coinbase’s Singapore country director, said safe agentic payments will require clear guardrails, including spending limits, restricted account permissions and explicit authorization requirements. Users should also be able to monitor activity and revoke access at any time, he said, given the potential for AI to create new opportunities for malicious actors. “While private or permissioned environments may offer additional controls for certain use cases, we should not lose sight of the potential of open blockchain networks to support more accessible, interoperable and efficient financial systems,” Ahmed said. JPMorgan and Hyundai Card are also exploring whether to extend their collaboration to other businesses within Hyundai Motor Group, whose broader operations were one reason the bank selected the credit card company as a partner, Toh said. No specific projects have been announced. Hyundai Motor Group holds a combined 78.04% stake in Hyundai Card through Hyundai Motor, Kia and Hyundai Commercial, according to the card issuer’s website. Hyundai Card has previously experimented with blockchain-based cross-border payments. In July, the company said it completed a proof-of-concept involving a $20,000 transfer using the USDT stablecoin between Hyundai Motor’s U.S. and Mexican subsidiaries, with the transfer and verification process taking an average of seven minutes. Kinexys has also been expanding its blockchain-based payments business. The JPMorgan unit said in August that it had processed more than $4 trillion in transactions since inception, averaging about $7 billion a day. Separately, JPMorgan launched a proof-of-concept for its dollar-denominated deposit token, JPMD, in June 2025, before making it available to institutional clients that November. JPMorgan Chase (JPM) said Tuesday that longtime CFO Jeremy Barnum will step down next year in the latest change among the top ranks of the country's largest bank as it prepares for CEO Jamie Dimon's eventual succession. Barnum, who has served as the bank's CFO since 2021, will be succeeded by Bregje de Best, CFO of JPMorgan's commercial and investment bank, after the company's first quarter earnings in April, according to a JPMorgan filing. Barnum will become vice chair, remaining with the bank until early 2028, JPMorgan said. Dimon added in a press release statement that Barnum had requested the transition after six years in the role. That tenure is slightly above average for a CFO at a large US company, according to a 2025 study by executive search firm Spencer Stuart, which found CFOs at S&P 500 companies had served an average of 4.8 years in their positions. The announcement comes less than a week after Allison Beer, JPMorgan's head of credit card and connected commerce, informed colleagues that she was leaving to pursue another opportunity, according to an internal JPMorgan memo. It also follows a broader leadership shake-up of Dimon's top lieutenants earlier this year when JPMorgan announced the retirement of Marianne Lake, the former head of its sprawling consumer bank and previously a leading candidate to succeed Dimon. The announcement of Lake's departure also came as JPMorgan said it was elevating executives Doug Petno and Troy Rohrbaugh to the role of co-president, signaling their leads to eventually take the reins from Dimon, who was expected to stay for three more years as CEO, according to an executive familiar with the matter who spoke to Yahoo Finance at the time. Barnum's planned transition and Lake's retirement are part of a broader effort to prepare JPMorgan's next generation of leadership, according to a person familiar with the bank's succession planning. The person characterized Beer's departure as separate, saying the credit card executive was seeking a broader leadership role than her current responsibilities at the bank. De Best, 43, joined JPMorgan in 2006 and has held senior positions across investment banking, markets and corporate banking. She will also join the firm's operating committee when she assumes the CFO role. Morgan Stanley analyst Manan Gosalia said Tuesday his team "do[es] not expect the CFO transition itself to have any impact on JPM's strategy or preliminary 2027 outlook." RBC Capital Markets analyst Gerard Cassidy also told clients Tuesday, in reaction to Barnum's departure, that senior management shake-ups are not unusual at JPMorgan. "We expect JPM's deep management bench will continue to enable the company to effectively manage through senior executive realignment," Cassidy said.
